targets.name: 3I/ATLAS, the interstellar comet
targets.note: Only the third object ever seen visiting our solar system from interstellar space. It was discovered in July 2025.
targets.summary: You are watching 90 real images of the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS taken between 01 Aug 2025 and 15 Dec 2025. By stacking all the images on the object, the stars smear away while the comet adds up to become visible. This object is only the third one ever seen visiting our solar system from interstellar space and was about 2.47 au away when the images were taken.

targets.name: Barnard's Star
targets.note: A red dwarf 6 light-years away. It crosses our sky faster than any other star.
targets.summary: Barnard's Star moved north at a rate of 9.2 ± 1.2 arcseconds a year, which matches the catalogue rate. This red dwarf is 6 light-years away and crosses our sky faster than any other star.

targets.name: Kapteyn's Star
targets.note: A very old star about 13 light-years away, with the second-fastest motion across the sky.
targets.summary: Kapteyn's Star was measured moving south-east at a rate of 8.3 ± 1.2 arcseconds a year, which matches the catalogue rate. This is a very old star about 13 light-years away, with the second-fastest motion across the sky.

targets.name: Groombridge 1830
targets.note: A star about 30 light-years away, one of the fastest-moving stars in our sky.
targets.summary: Groombridge 1830 moved at a rate of 6.8 ± 1.2 arcseconds a year toward the south-south-east. This star is about 30 light-years away and is one of the fastest-moving stars in our sky.

targets.name: Lacaille 9352
targets.note: A red dwarf about 10.7 light-years away in the southern sky.
targets.summary: Lacaille 9352 moved east at a rate of 8.0 ± 1.2 arcseconds a year, which is about 1/233 the width of a full moon. This is a red dwarf about 10.7 light-years away in the southern sky.

targets.name: Wolf 359
targets.note: One of the closest stars to the Sun, about 7.9 light-years away.
targets.summary: Wolf 359 moved at a rate of 4.0 ± 0.5 arcseconds a year, which matches the catalogue rate. This star is one of the closest to the Sun, located about 7.9 light-years away.

targets.name: Teegarden's Star
targets.note: A small red dwarf 12.5 light-years away with Earth-sized planets.
targets.summary: Teegarden's Star was measured moving south-east at a rate of 5.1 ± 0.5 arcseconds a year, which matches previous records and covers about 1/366 of the full Moon's width each year. Teegarden's Star is a small red dwarf 12.5 light-years away with Earth-sized planets.

targets.name: WISE J184125.47+095436.5
targets.note: A star that NASA's WISE telescope flagged as variable years earlier. Can SPHEREx see it change?
targets.summary: WISE J184125.47+095436.5 faded by 0.66 magnitudes between September 2025 and September 2026. This star was previously flagged as variable by NASA's WISE telescope, and SPHEREx has now confirmed this change.

targets.name: Pleiades
targets.note: A young star cluster about 440 light-years away, wrapped in dust that reflects starlight.
targets.summary: No measurable changes were detected in the sky between these observations of the Pleiades. This is a young star cluster about 440 light-years away, wrapped in dust that reflects starlight.

targets.name: Crab Nebula
targets.note: The remains of a star that exploded and was seen from Earth in the year 1054.
targets.summary: No measurable changes were detected in the sky between these observations of the Crab Nebula. This object is the remains of a star that exploded and was seen from Earth in the year 1054.

targets.name: Orion Nebula
targets.note: A cloud 1,300 light-years away where new stars are forming.
targets.summary: No measurable changes were found in the view between September 2025 and September 2026. This target is a cloud 1,300 light-years away where new stars are forming.
